quote: Teachers sometimes call this the false *se* (*se espurio*): it's just *le* or *les* in disguise, nothing to do with the *se* in *se llama*.
problem: Learners in Latin America will meet se los dije for I told them, with the plural moved onto lo. The script says this se has no plural, which is right, but it gives no warning about a form they'll hear and misread as several things.
authority: RAE, Gramática, Los pronombres dativos (via search summary): the plural is moved to the accusative, very common in many countries; Moreno de Alba 2013. Colombian use is my judgement
replacement: Teachers sometimes call this the false *se* (*se espurio*): it's just *le* or *les* in disguise, nothing to do with the *se* in *se llama*. In Latin America you'll also hear *se los dije* for I told them: the plural slips onto *lo*. Understand it, but say *se lo dije*.

replacement: You're asking where it happens, not where a thing sits: *es*. You'll hear *está* in casual speech, but *es* is always right.

quote: The verb stays in the he/she form whoever you mean, because you don't mean anyone.

authority: Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), passive and impersonal se
replacement: With no thing to match, the verb stays in the he/she form, because you don't mean anyone in particular.

quote: With more than one thing, the verb goes plural: *se vende carro*, but *se venden carros*.

authority: Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), passive and impersonal se
replacement: When there is a thing, the verb matches it, because the thing is really the subject: *se vende carro*, but *se venden carros*.

quote: No dudo que tengas razón.
problem: Correct, common Spanish is struck through as a mistake. Textbooks teach the indicative here, and that is a fair default, but negated dudar admits both moods: the indicative asserts, the subjunctive concedes. The course itself uses the subjunctive here: all 9 bank rows with *no dudo que* (u44-0915 to u44-1533) are subjunctive, and none is indicative, so the learner is told a form is wrong and later drilled on nothing else. Tested through the real card code: typing it fails with the hint "Check the verb ending: when does it happen?"
authority: Decisive: internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u44.json. Also Nueva gramatica ch. 25 and Butt and Benjamin ch. 16, from memory, not checkable online; native speaker reports on tomisimo and Lawless Spanish

quote: The flip side: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb comes back: *No dudo que tienes razón*.
problem: Presents the indicative as the only option. A good rule keeps the plain verb as the default and says the other exists, which also follows from the course's own model: stating it as a fact versus granting it.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16)
replacement: The flip side: *No dudo que* says you are sure, so the plain verb is the natural choice: *No dudo que tienes razón*. You will also meet the wish form here, often before a *pero*: *No dudo que tengas razón, pero...* Both are correct.

quote: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it takes the indicative.
problem: States the indicative as obligatory. Same issue as the rule.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement: *No dudo que* usually takes the indicative, because it is certainty, but the subjunctive is also correct.

quote: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb comes back: *tienes*.
problem: The fill-in offers *tienes* or *tengas* with accept empty, so the correct *tengas* is marked wrong. Either accept both or remove the item.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement: Set accept to ["No dudo que tengas razón."] and why to: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb is the natural choice: *tienes*.

quote: *Puede que* + wish form
problem: The bank drills 18 rows with *no es cierto que* or *no es verdad que* and 14 with *es imposible que* in u29, for example u29-0600 and u29-0624, tagged g:subj-doubt. No script in the course names either frame. x:fact-value teaches that *es verdad que* takes the plain verb and never says that denying it flips the mood.
authority: Internal; Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement:
*Puede que* + wish form

The same goes when you deny a fact or rule it out: *No es cierto que el café pierda plata.* *Es imposible que lo sepa.*

quote: No dudo que tengas razón.
problem: B1 file, flagged because it conflicts with B2. p:concede-pero and nine bank rows at u44 use this construction as correct. Marking it wrong sets up the contradiction.
authority: Two lessons contradict each other. Learner references mostly give indicative after no dudo que, while the subjunctive also occurs, especially when conceding, so neither form is wrong. I found no NGLE text on this; check NGLE ch. 25 and DPD dudar.
replacement: {"wrong": "Dudo que tienes razón.", "right": "Dudo que tengas razón.", "why": "Almost. *Dudo que* takes the wish form. It is *no dudo que* that can keep the plain verb."}

quote: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it takes the indicative.
problem: True as the default, but stated as an absolute that a later lesson breaks.
authority: Two lessons contradict each other. Learner references mostly give indicative after no dudo que, while the subjunctive also occurs, especially when conceding, so neither form is wrong. I found no NGLE text on this; check NGLE ch. 25 and DPD dudar.
replacement: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it usually takes the indicative. Later you will meet it with the subjunctive too, when someone grants a point before a *pero*.

quote: No dudo que tengas razón.
problem: Marked wrong, but no dudo que takes either mood. The subjunctive is at least as common in careful writing, and both are in the Academy grammar. A C1 reader will meet it constantly and believe it is a mistake. Delete the pitfall.
authority: RAE, Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), chapter on mood (no dudar que admits both moods); Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, chapter on the subjunctive

quote: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it takes the indicative.
problem: States one option as the only one. See the pitfall claim on the same node.
authority: RAE, Nueva gramática de la lengua española (2009), chapter on mood
replacement: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it usually takes the indicative, but the subjunctive is correct too: *No dudo que tengas razón.*

quote: The flip side: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb comes back: *No dudo que tienes razón*.
problem: No dudo que takes either mood. No dudo que tengas razón is standard and common, so the rule is false as stated and the pitfall built on it marks correct Spanish wrong.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish ch. 16 (no dudar que with indicative or subjunctive); Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (RAE/ASALE 2009) ch. 25
replacement: The flip side: *No dudo que* means you are sure, so the plain verb usually comes back: *No dudo que tienes razón*. You'll also read *No dudo que tengas razón*; both are correct.

quote: {"wrong": "No dudo que tengas razón.", "right": "No dudo que tienes razón.", "why": "Almost. *No dudo que* means you are sure, so there is nothing to step back from: the plain verb stays."}
problem: The "wrong" sentence is correct Spanish.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish ch. 16; Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (RAE/ASALE 2009) ch. 25
replacement: {"wrong": "Puede que llueve hoy.", "right": "Puede que llueva hoy.", "why": "Almost. *Puede que* only says it might happen, so the verb takes the wish form."}

quote: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it takes the indicative.
problem: Same over-claim as the rule.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish ch. 16
replacement: *No dudo que* is certainty, so it usually takes the indicative, though the subjunctive is also correct.

quote: Llámame antes que salgas.
problem: Correct Spanish is struck through. *Antes que* and *antes de que* are both valid before a clause. The real slip English speakers make is dropping *que*.
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry antes (equal examples: Llegara antes que anochezca, Llegara antes de que anochezca), read via search snippet of rae.es/dpd/antes
replacement: {"wrong":"Llámame antes de salgas.","right":"Llámame antes de que salgas.","why":"Almost. When a new person does the second action, you need *que*: *antes de que*."}

quote: *Antes de que* needs the *de*, then the wish form *salgas*.
problem: Claims the *de* is required. Accept should also include *Llámame antes que salgas.*
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry antes
replacement: *Antes de que* is followed by the wish form: *salgas*.

quote: When the same person does both things, drop *que* and use the plain verb: *Abro temprano para encontrar todo listo.* *Llámame antes de salir.*
problem: Same collision: here plain verb means infinitive.
authority: Internal
replacement: When the same person does both things, drop *que* and use the infinitive: *Abro temprano para encontrar todo listo.* *Llámame antes de salir.*

quote: When the same person does both things, *que* disappears and the verb stays plain.
problem: Same collision.
authority: Internal
replacement: When the same person does both things, *que* disappears and you use the infinitive.

quote: Almost. If you do both things yourself, skip *que* and use the plain verb.
problem: Same collision.
authority: Internal
replacement: Almost. If you do both things yourself, skip *que* and use the infinitive.

quote: The second action belongs to someone else, so its verb takes the wish form: *veas*, *note*, *salgas*, *llegue*.
problem: Gives the wrong cause. A change of subject explains *que* versus the infinitive. It does not explain the mood: *Llamo porque vienes* has a change of subject and takes the indicative. The mood comes from the second action being not yet real.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on mood (25)
replacement: The second action belongs to someone else, so you need *que*. It hasn't happened yet when you plan it, so its verb takes the form you know from *quiero que*: *veas*, *note*, *salgas*, *llegue*.

quote: Llámame antes de que salgas.
problem: Tested through scriptCard: this correct answer is rejected. Hint shown for *Llámame antes que salgas*: "A small word is missing."
authority: RAE, Diccionario panhispanico de dudas, entry antes
replacement: Add to accept: "Llámame antes que salgas."

quote: Dijo que vendrá.
problem: *Dijo que vendrá* is correct whenever the coming is still ahead of the speaker now, and it is very common in Latin America. The rule that the future must shift is false as an absolute. The form is only wrong when the event lies in the past story.
authority: Nueva gramatica, ch. 24, double access, from memory; standard accounts agree the form needs the present perspective
replacement: {"wrong":"Ayer Vale dijo que vendrá, pero no vino.","right":"Ayer Vale dijo que vendría, pero no vino.","why":"Almost. She did not come, so the coming belongs to the past story: use the would form. *Dijo que vendrá* only works if it is still ahead of you now."}

quote: Teachers call this reported speech with backshift: the pluperfect stands in for the past and the conditional for the future, seen from a moment in the past.
problem: Contradicts u25 g:reported-past-basic, which says "Something already in the past stays put: *Joaquín se fue* → *Dijo que Joaquín se fue*." Here *Llamé* must become *había llamado*. Neither script says both are right. In Colombian speech the simple past is the more usual choice.
authority: Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola, chapter on tense concord (24); usage
replacement: Teachers call this reported speech with backshift: the pluperfect stands in for the past and the conditional for the future, seen from a moment in the past. In everyday Latin American speech the simple past often stays: *Dijo que llamó tres veces*. Both are right.

quote: Almost. A rate such as "three times a day" is always *por*.
problem: False. *Tres veces al día* and *una vez a la semana* are at least as common, and the bank itself has 45 such rows against 10 with *por* (u03-0538, u09-0013, u35-0090). A learner who trusts "always" will think the commonest form is wrong.
authority: Usage; internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u03.json and u09.json
replacement: Almost. A rate never takes *para*. Say *por día* or, just as often, *al día*: *tres veces al día*.

quote: For me, the café in Altamira is the best.
problem: Altamira is a company, not a town.
authority: Story bible
replacement: For me, Altamira's coffee is the best.

quote: For me, the proposal is obviously good.
problem: *Muy* is dropped. The owner's rule is an exact translation.
authority: Owner rule
replacement: For me, the proposal is obviously very good.

quote: *a swap*: *lo cambié por otro*, trading one thing for another
problem: The node title promises "por for time", but the rule gives only rate, means and swap. The commonest English use of "for", a stretch of time, is taught nowhere as a por or para question. Learners will write para dos horas. Spanish often needs no word at all.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish ch. 34 (por and para with time); Nueva gramatica de la lengua espanola (RAE/ASALE 2009)
replacement:
*a swap*: *lo cambié por otro*, trading one thing for another
*how long*, when English says for: *Trabajé ahí por dos años*. Often Spanish needs no word at all: *Estudié dos horas*. Not *para*.

quote: Spanish always keeps *que* and the changed ending.
problem: False for *recomendar*, *aconsejar* and *sugerir*, which also take an infinitive: *Te recomiendo hablar con un abogado*. The bank has it: u21-0749 *Te aconsejo hablar con un abogado*, u31-0864, u35-0049.
authority: Butt and Benjamin, A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish, subjunctive chapter (16); internal contradiction with app/content/bank/u21.json
replacement: Spanish uses *que* and the form you know from *quiero que*. With *recomendar*, *aconsejar* and *sugerir* you will also meet the infinitive: *Te recomiendo hablar con un abogado.* Both are right.

quote: *Te recomiendo* + *que* + a new verb form.
problem: At u32 the form is not new: the learner has used it since u21 and in every script from u28 to u30. It is presented as new, with its endings retaught, and renamed "asking form". Three days later it is "the other vowel", three days after that "the wish form".
authority: Internal: g:subj-wanting (u21), g:subj-opinion-negated (u28), g:subj-cuando-future (u32 d4), g:subj-purpose-full (u32 d7)
replacement: *Te recomiendo* + *que* + the form you already know from *quiero que*.

quote: The verb after *que* is for the other person's action, and it changes its ending to the "asking" form.
problem: Same issue: a new name for a known form.
authority: Internal
replacement: The verb after *que* is for the other person's action, and it takes the same form you use after *quiero que*.

quote: Te recomiendo que duermas más.
problem: Tested through scriptCard: this correct answer is rejected. Hint shown for *Te recomiendo dormir más*: "A small word is missing."
authority: Internal: u21-0749
replacement: Add to accept: "Te recomiendo dormir más."
